title: Unified bound for binary search trees
formal: Does a deterministic online BST algorithm exist with total access cost \(O(n\log(2+n)+U(X))\) for every sequence \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in[n]^m\), where \[U(X)=\sum_{t=1}^{m}\log_2\!\left(2+\min\left\{n,\min_{1\le s<t}(t-s+|x_t-x_s|)\right\}\right)?\] The minimum over an empty set is \(+\infty\); the initialization term is independent of \(m\).
definitions: The keys are the fixed ranks \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A BST has one node per key in symmetric order. Each access begins with a pointer at the root; primitive costs are moving it to a parent or child, performing a rotation incident to the pointer, and visiting the requested key. Other input-dependent state must be kept in the tree with constant-size fields per node. The algorithm sees requests only as they arrive; it may restructure the tree but may not use arbitrary jumps, an auxiliary search structure or advance knowledge. Begin with a balanced tree, constructed within the initialization allowance. There are no insertions or deletions. The target uses the elapsed-access definition of the unified bound in the 2024 paper; the cap by \(n\) and the additive constants cover first accesses. A uniform algorithm and universal multiplicative constant must work for all \(n,m,X\).
why: The unified bound asks one search tree to exploit temporal and rank locality together, beyond proving separate working-set and dynamic-finger guarantees.

context_blocks.text: Iacono introduced comparison-based structures satisfying the unified bound. Achieving it within a single BST remains the source question.

Skip-splay and the group-access construction obtain \(O(U(X)+m\log\log n)\), apart from initialization. The 2024 paper explicitly notes that an older cache-tree claim was questioned and retains the exact BST target as open.

sentences: A search should be cheap when its key is close in rank to a recently requested key.
The unified bound combines this spatial locality with temporal locality.
The target requires a single online binary search tree.
Known BST bounds include an extra logarithmic-logarithmic term per access.
The cited source distinguishes an earlier disputed claim from an established solution.
